{{Short description|American physicist and professor (1939–2020)}}
'''Peter John Brancazio''' (March 22, 1939 – April 25, 2020) was an American professor of physics at [[Brooklyn College]] for more than 30 years, whose observatory he temporarily headed. He was best known for his work on physics in sports.

== Personal life ==
Brancazio was born in [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]], [[Queens]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. His interest in physics was sparked when his girlfriend and future wife Ronnie Kramer gave him a telescope.

He studied [[engineering science]] at [[New York University]] (NYU) and graduated with a [[bachelor's degree]] in 1959. He later studied at [[Columbia University]] and gained his [[Master's degree|master's]] in [[nuclear engineering]] a year later. Brancazio started teaching physics at [[Brooklyn College]] in 1963 while studying [[astrophysics]] at NYU, working toward a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]]. He taught physics at the college until his retirement in 1997. After that, he taught adult education courses at Brooklyn College and Queens College for a while. Finally, from 1999 to 2019, he taught courses on religion, science and astronomy at [[Hutton House]], a branch of [[Long Island University]]. In recognition of his achievements, he was awarded a Tow Professorship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter Brancazio |url=https://www.cuny.edu/blog/memorial/peter-brancazio/ |access-date=2023-10-26 |website=The City University of New York |language=en}}</ref>

Peter Brancazio died from [[COVID-19]] on April 25, 2020, in [[Manhasset, New York]], amid [[COVID-19 pandemic in New York (state)|its pandemic]]. He left two sons, his wife, and several grandchildren.<ref name="Sandomir">{{cite news |last1=Sandomir |first1=Richard |title=Peter Brancazio, Who Explored the Physics of Sports, Dies at 81 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/16/obituaries/peter-brancazio-dead-coronavirus.html |access-date=27 September 2021 |work=The New York Times |date=16 May 2020 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200517172715/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/16/obituaries/peter-brancazio-dead-coronavirus.html |archive-date=17 May 2020 |url-access=limited}}</ref>

== Work ==
In 1981, he published his first work on sports physics in the ''[[American Journal of Physics]]'', in which he found the perfect throw angle in baseball.<ref name="Sandomir"/> In 1983, his work on the physics of judging a [[Fly ball (baseball)|fly ball]] were noted by the ''[[New Scientist]]''.<ref>{{cite book |title=New Scientist |date=24 February 1983 |publisher=Reed Business Information |page=564 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dGloQlpCO_4C&pg=PA564}}</ref> In 1984, his book ''Sport Science'' was published,<ref name="Sandomir"/> where he "claim[ed] to have discovered the way to make a pure shooter by following the laws of physics"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ballard |first1=Chris |title=The Art of a Beautiful Game: The Thinking Fan's Tour of the NBA |date=3 November 2009 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-1-4391-4117-5 |page=28 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KwzZwJWBO_EC&pg=PA28}}</ref> and "discuss[ed] a variety of physics concepts using sports".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Minton |first1=Roland |title=Golf by the Numbers: How Stats, Math, and Physics Affect Your Game |date=September 2012 |publisher=JHU Press |isbn=978-1-4214-0315-1 |page=vii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=puAB92Y8gnUC |language=en}}</ref>

Although he was personally more interested in basketball, he was best known for his work on baseball. A number of terms he introduced are now part of the technical vocabulary of baseball.<ref name="Sandomir"/>

== Publications ==
* ''The Nature of Physics'', McMillian 1975, ISBN 9780023135002
* ''Sport Science: Physical Laws and Optimum Performance'', Simon & Schuster 1985, ISBN 9780671554385
